name: Fatima Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government. What you say is confidential. What happened at work yesterday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was trying to explain to a childcare centre why three months of fees did not match its bank deposits, then I found a batch that had been dated a week late. I'm 43, an experienced mid-level accountant at Fieldstone Accounts, about average at the job, with a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification. I like helping a manager understand the payroll before wages go out; I hate learning about a late receipt after the return is ready to sign.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What about home, savings and the technology you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Tomas repairs buses, and our children are six and ten; both leave their shoes by the door in a heap. We have a mortgage, my accounting pay is high for this job, about eleven months of bills saved and plenty of similar firms nearby. I use AI every day to sort fee records and draft questions, then check the bank proof myself. I favour a staff voice and rules for automated decisions, but I also like trying a tool early when it can show its errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the childcare managers that a tidy first pass is welcome if we keep a person who can explain the bank line. I would show the late-dated batch before saying the software found a saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two wages and eleven months saved make the mortgage secure in this quiet world. I still need to check the fee records, but I don't expect my hours to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for daily fee sorting and compare the odd entries with bank proof. In the first year I'd move one hundred monthly from salary into our emergency fund and spend a paid hour showing a junior how I found the late batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our income. Teaching the junior a real mistake feels more useful than another glossy software update.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the batch date slip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre entered Friday's card payments on Monday, and the system treated them as new fees. I checked the merchant statement against the bank date before changing the return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I use the approved system at work and the firm should pay for business software. My household reserve is for our children and mortgage.

I would keep a **human explainer** on late entries.
think: Our **mortgage feels secure** with high pay and eleven months saved.
I do not expect my **hours to change** in a plateau.
do: Keep checking **fee batches** after daily AI sorting.
Save **one hundred monthly** from pay into our emergency fund.
Teach a junior the **late-batch check** during paid work.
feel: She feels **calm** about stable wages and a secure mortgage.
S0.quote: Teaching the junior a real mistake feels more useful than another glossy software update.
fieldNote: She uses AI **daily** but teaches the junior a bank-date error from a real childcare account.
Her high wage and eleven-month cushion keep the household **secure** through mild automation.

steps.text: Keep checking childcare fee batches and teach junior late-batch checks on paid time
Save one hundred monthly from salary into emergency fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm to show the new system's missed fees, not just the number of returns it finishes. If the partners reduce a team, staff should see the plan before a rota changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI can check and write much of the work I do, and I expect our team to lose a reviewer shift. I might keep my own hours because I know the clients. Average skill is no promise, so my wage could be reduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd test the new approved checker on fifteen closed childcare returns during paid time if the firm agrees, keeping an error log with the senior. In the first year of steady change, if my hours are cut, I'd apply for posted accounting roles at the nearby firms and keep my Fieldstone pay until I have a written offer with wage and start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours, despite the savings. I would want the junior team to see the error log as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm refuses paid testing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue the approved daily sorting and source checks, not run an unapproved system on live childcare files. I'd ask the staff forum to record the refusal and the proposed rota change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family need from a new job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written wage covering the mortgage and school costs, with a start time that lets Tomas or me collect our six-year-old. I would not hand in notice because a firm says it might have an opening.

I would demand a **visible rota plan** before team cuts.
think: The **reviewer shift** could disappear because AI can check and write much of our childcare accounts work.
Eleven months saved provides **search time**, not another wage.
do: Test **fifteen closed returns** on paid time with senior review if approved.
Keep **approved daily checks** if trial funding is refused.
Seek **posted accounting work** after cuts with written pay covering mortgage/school costs and pickup-compatible start; retain Fieldstone pay until offer confirmed.
feel: She feels **anxious** because her own paid hours could shrink.
S1.quote: Average skill is no promise, so my wage could be reduced.
fieldNote: Her trial needs **paid time** and old files, while daily source checks continue if it is refused.
She asks the **staff forum** to record any refusal and rota change before seeking a written outside offer.

steps.text: Test fifteen closed childcare returns on paid time with senior review if approved
Keep approved fee checks if trial funding refused
Seek posted accounts after cuts with written mortgage wage/start/pickup; keep Fieldstone pay until offer confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell staff that full AGI in 2028 can do our accounts and tax thinking work, while hands-on robots arrive around 2031. We need a signed plan for who answers a childcare centre when a machine is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Fieldstone to remove some accounting posts when fee checking becomes cheap, and my role could be one of them. Tomas's bus repair is hands-on and may face robots later, so our eleven months saved would not cover two very long searches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd add two hundred monthly to our job-loss cash from salary and ask the staff forum for a month's notice before cuts. In the first year after 2028, if my post ends, I'd apply for posted salaried finance posts at local childcare groups and keep any paid Fieldstone work until a written wage and start date cover our fixed bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though I expect posts to go. We have time and nearby employers to try before the mortgage is late, but I will not pretend my role is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use public support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a search ran beyond our reserve and we qualified for temporary mortgage help, I'd apply. I would not plan our budget as though approval were certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the forum to put in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A month's notice, a named human signer and paid help finding a new post. I'd bring the childcare centre's late-batch example so this is about a real error, not a slogan.

say: I would ask for **one month’s notice** and a named signer.
I would request **paid placement help** before posts go.
think: My **accounting post** could be among the cuts when cheap AGI handles fee checks in 2028.
Tomas’s **bus-repair work** may face robots around 2031.
do: Save **two hundred monthly** into job-loss cash.
Ask the **staff forum** for notice and paid placement.
Seek **posted childcare finance** after job loss while keeping paid Fieldstone hours; request eligible mortgage help only if reserves run out.
feel: She feels **anxious** about a realistic job cut, with usable savings.
S2.quote: We have time and nearby employers to try before the mortgage is late, but I will not pretend my role is safe.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 desk cuts** from later hands-on robot risk to Tomas’s bus work.
She would request **mortgage help** only after reserve exhaustion and eligibility, while first using savings and nearby vacancies.

steps.text: Add two hundred monthly from salary into job-loss cash
Ask staff forum for month notice and paid job placement
Seek posted childcare finance after job loss; keep paid Fieldstone hours until written bill-covering wage/start confirmed
Request temporary mortgage help only if search outlasts reserve and eligibility is confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years allows a choice about whether to train for something clients still need, instead of guessing after a cut. I would ask employers to name the paid posts before people buy courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031 I would still have two children to support and a mortgage, and AGI could do even the childcare accounts checks I enjoy. I could change direction with time, but I would need a real salary, not just a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the local college whether it has a posted paid opening to teach basic accounts and whether it requires a teaching certificate. If one does, I'd take the certificate only with funded fees and paid study time while keeping my Fieldstone wage; in the first year after 2031, if my accounting hours fall, I'd apply for that advertised college role only with a written wage and start date covering the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years gives me time to see whether teaching actually pays. I will not spend our household reserve on a qualification for a job that has not been posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be able to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already show juniors how to trace a late fee batch, but I would need practice with a whole group. I'd ask to run one paid training session at Fieldstone before committing to a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the college has no posted role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current paid accounts work and the monthly savings transfer, and I would not buy a certificate. Tomas and I need a wage while the children are in school.

say: I would seek a **posted paid teaching role** before buying training.
I would ask for **paid group practice** at Fieldstone first.
think: At **48 in 2031**, I still need wages for two children and the mortgage.
A **certificate alone** cannot replace my accounting salary.
do: Run a **paid group session** at Fieldstone if assigned.
Take a **required teaching certificate** only for a posted role with funded fees, paid study and Fieldstone wage retained.
Apply for **advertised college teaching** after 2031 hours fall.
feel: She feels **anxious**, with time to test paid teaching demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets us pay down the mortgage and see what work people will still pay a person to explain. The firm should keep the junior learning path open, not close it for a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 I would still want paid work, but the children may be out of school and the mortgage could be much smaller. AGI reaches my desk then, while robots around 2039 may change Tomas's bus-repair work later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay one hundred and fifty extra monthly off the mortgage while both wages hold, and take paid group-teaching hours at Fieldstone if the manager funds them. In the first year after 2036, if accounting work no longer funds my salary, I'd apply for posted salaried college finance or teaching roles and keep current paid hours until a written wage and start date are confirmed. Those paid groups would let me keep practising how to teach adults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about needing a wage at 53, even with a smaller loan. A decade could make the family less fragile, but it does not create a posted job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Tomas loses work before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra principal payment and hold the cash for household bills. I would not put the children's schooling fund into a course or a new software tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early if the loan were small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, eleven months saved is a cushion, not a pension. I would rather stay paid, either here or at a college if a real post opens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because some accounting posts could go before our children are grown. A month's notice, paid placement help and a posted childcare finance job with written terms would help. Eleven months of savings can buy time, but it cannot buy an employer's signature.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a childcare manager challenges a wrong automated fee total. The parent waiting for a refund deserves a person who can open the bank record.

headlineQuote: The parent waiting for a refund deserves a person who can open the bank record.
portrait: Fatima, **43**, is an average-skilled mid-level accountant at Fieldstone with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification.
Her **high pay**, eleven-month reserve and Tomas’s bus-repair wage support two school-age children and a mortgage.
She uses AI **daily** on childcare fee accounts, with many nearby firms if she must seek a new post.
She fears **2028 post cuts** and tests a paid teaching path only when a real college role exists.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove accounting posts before her children are grown.
whatWouldHelp: **One month’s notice**, paid placement and a posted childcare finance role with written terms would help.
